statement: The draft gets the main idea right: code by hash, a file system made of roots, and a run journal. But storage mixes the shared content-addressed substrate with one of its consumers (the file system), and it treats block writes and per-block pins as domain events when the real facts are which roots are held and why. The audit context also has two log-mechanics items (upcasting and retention) that need reshaping. Upcasting is a pure read-time function, not an event, and retention has to be a policy that releases payload roots, otherwise H6 and H12 cannot be resolved.

renames.why: Pins are recursive holds on a root CID (a file system root, a release module, a journal payload, an artifact bundle) with a reason and holder. Nobody pins single blocks, and per-block events would be millions of rows.
Pairs with ContentRootPinned. Releasing a root only makes its blocks candidates for garbage collection; other roots that share blocks still keep them alive.
This covers both missing blocks and blocks whose bytes do not hash to their CID (corruption, a bad replica). Either one blocks replay and audit the same way.

splits.why: One is a decision by an admin or compliance (how long run journals, model responses and connection payloads are kept). The other is the fact that a period ended for a stream, and the policy reacting to it emits ContentRootReleased for its payload roots. The small hash-chained events stay; only the referenced blobs go.

missing.why: MakeDirectory is a real effect and produces a new root. Without this event the file events cannot replay to the same root CIDs.

remove.why: The block store is a content-addressed substrate, not an event-sourced aggregate. A block's CID proves its content, and putting a block is idempotent and very high volume. What matters is which event or pin references it. Logging every put would double the log and add nothing (I proposed this event in round 1 and withdraw it).

It duplicates FileWritten, FileDeleted and DirectoryCreated. Instead each file event carries previous_root and new_root CIDs (previous_root acts as the optimistic concurrency check), with the domain name kept as Priya wants. FileSystemRestored also carries both roots.

Upcasting is a pure function applied when old events are read. Appending an event each time would be noise and would change on every rebuild. Schema versions belong in each event's envelope (a type tag plus a version, like the hub's decoder_set).

moves.why: Read models are rebuilt from the log plus aggregate snapshots stored as blocks, which is store mechanics rather than compliance. Keep it as an operational event that records projector version and log position, next to garbage collection.

context_changes.change: Split storage into `content` (ContentRootPinned, ContentRootReleased, GarbageCollectionSweepCompleted, BlockIntegrityFailed, ProjectionRebuilt) and `files` (FileWritten, DirectoryCreated, FileDeleted, FileSystemSnapshotTagged, FileSystemRestored).
context_changes.why: Content addressing is the shared substrate under packages, runs, conversations, artifacts and files, with its own language (CID, root, pin, reachability). The file system is one consumer with its own language (path, root, change, by whom).

context_changes.change: Split outputs into `artifacts` (ArtifactVersionSaved, ArtifactShared) and `databases` (DatabaseStatementExecuted, DatabaseSnapshotTaken, DataclipInvoked).
context_changes.why: Artifacts are immutable bundles that should be stored as a UnixFS directory, with the event carrying only the bundle root CID so unchanged files dedupe across versions. Databases are mutable SQLite state outside the log, with a different consistency and replay model (H18).

hotspot_positions.position: Journal Now, Random and Flip inline because they are a few bytes. ReadFile does not need its bytes copied: the file system is immutable, so the journal records the root CID and the file's content CID, and replay reads the same blocks. Fetch bodies, model responses and other large results go to the block store and the event holds the CID. Durability uses group commit: put the payload blocks, then append the events, then fsync once per batch before resuming any run in the batch.

Provenance lives only in the event, never in the block. A mocked result can share a CID with a real one because identical bytes dedupe. So EffectMocked must stay a distinct event type (or an unmissable decision field) and replay takes 'was this real' from the event. Projections that show effect results must carry the decision with them.

Use crypto-shredding. Encrypt blocks that may hold personal data (messages, effect results, model responses, connection payloads) with a per-workspace data key, plus per-subject keys where a subject can be identified. Dedup is convergent only inside a workspace. Events keep only ciphertext CIDs and non-personal metadata, so erasure means destroying a key and appending PersonalDataErased. The hash chain stays valid, and garbage collection can then sweep the unreadable blocks.

One stream per aggregate (workspace config, file system, run, conversation, connection, artifact, trigger, schedule) with a per-stream sequence and a previous-event CID, as in untethered substrate. Appends are optimistic on expected sequence. Total order is needed only within a workspace: a single writer per workspace log assigns the global position, and hash chaining happens at the workspace log level, with AuditLogCheckpointSigned signing the head CID periodically. Wall-clock time is data on the event, never the order. Aggregate snapshots are blocks keyed by (stream, sequence), are caches and not events, and can always be rebuilt.

Never rewrite the log. Every event has a type tag and a schema version in dag-json. Upcasters are pure, tested functions vN to vN+1 applied on read. When a projector changes, its read model is rebuilt from position 0 or from a snapshot taken by a compatible projector version. A version can only be retired after a signed checkpoint proves no live retained events use it.
Traces become a projection of the run journal plus decisions. They are rebuildable and can be sampled or exported, but they are never the source.

Secret values must never reach the block store, not even hashed: a plain CID of a low-entropy secret can be brute-forced, and its blocks dedupe across uses. Record a reference instead, such as secret name plus the SecretSet sequence or a keyed HMAC placeholder like today's hash placeholder. On replay, re-inject the value for that version from the secret store. If that version was rotated away, the replay stops with a clear divergence instead of using the new value.

Resolve every @name exactly once at RunStarted. ReferencesPinned stores the name to release to module CID map as one dag-json block, and the event holds its CID. Replay uses only that map and never asks the hub. Every module block referenced by a retained journal is pinned in the local content store, so replay never depends on hub availability. The hub keeps module blocks of signed releases forever.

Inline if the encoded payload is 4 KiB or less, otherwise use a block and a CID (chunked UnixFS above 256 KiB). Blocks are written before the event that references them, so an event never points at a missing block. Unreferenced blocks from crashed writers are swept after a 24h grace period. Garbage collection is mark and sweep from a LiveRoots read model: current workspace file system roots, tagged snapshots, release modules, in-flight runs, retained journals, conversations and connection payloads, all artifact versions, and legal holds. Retention releases roots; it never deletes blocks directly.

Record every delivery, but cheaply. Store raw bodies as blocks (repeated payloads dedupe) and batch high-volume sources: one ConnectionEventReceived per batch referencing a block that lists N delivery CIDs, with matched deliveries named individually by TriggerMatched. Unmatched payloads get a short retention class; the small events stay.

The SQLite file is a projection cache, not the source. DatabaseStatementExecuted records the statement, its bound parameters (large ones by CID) and the changed row count. Nondeterministic SQL (random(), datetime('now')) is rejected or rewritten with values from the journal. DatabaseSnapshotTaken stores the database file as chunked blocks at a log position, so rebuild means restoring the snapshot and replaying the statements after it, and old statements can then be released by retention.

Revert is a new WorkspaceSourceChanged pointing at an earlier source CID. History is never rewound. Effects already performed stay in the log. The same applies to the file system: FileSystemRestored moves the head to an old root with a new event and keeps the intermediate roots until retention releases them.

new_hotspots.text: Two stores and no distributed transaction: the block store and the event log commit separately. What ordering and checks (blocks first, verify every referenced CID exists before appending) do we enforce, and who repairs a BlockIntegrityFailed found during replay or audit export?

Dedup scope: global dedup across workspaces saves space but lets one tenant confirm that another holds a given file (confirmation-of-file attack) and conflicts with per-workspace encryption keys. Is the block store per workspace, per organization, or global only for public content such as hub modules?

Files are a single raw block today, so every Append and edit rewrites the whole file, and large uploads and model outputs are one huge block. Chunking (fixed 256 KiB or content-defined) changes every file CID, so the scheme must be chosen once and recorded as part of the file system's identity.

Can a signed release be retracted (malicious or leaked-secret module)? Pinned runs still need its blocks to replay, but new resolutions must skip it. Retraction should be a signed event, and garbage collection must keep the blocks while any retained journal references them.
